National Conversation | Place preference & deprivation

Neighbourhood deprivation changes the environments people evaluate; core place valuations remain shared, with only small absolute Theme × IMD shifts.

Place-based preferences and free-text explanations from across England.

Liked & disliked map pins | IoD 2025 | POIs | text themes

Introduction

What we know - and what we don’t

Urban inequality research has extensively documented differences in access to neighbourhood amenities, green space and infrastructure.

Much less is known about whether the same kinds of environments are valued differently in deprived and affluent contexts - or whether preferences are shared despite unequal contexts.

National Conversation pins across England (72,298 England pins | 79,182 participants).

Contribution

Three things that are easy to conflate

Using place pins and free-text explanations, we distinguish:

1. Neighbourhood context

How deprived is the place? What amenities surround it?

2. Environments evaluated

Which kinds of places do people pin as liked or disliked?

3. Preferences themselves

Given the same place type, do valuations differ by deprivation?

The novelty is not “people like parks.” It is whether that valuation holds across deprivation - or breaks down.
Research questions

Three questions

RQ1

How do neighbourhood environments differ across deprivation? Spatial / IMD context

RQ2

Which neighbourhood environments are associated with positive and negative place experiences? POI + NLP - what people value

RQ3

Do these preferences differ with the deprivation of the evaluated place? Interaction chapter - the novelty. Deprivation of places, not (necessarily) of people.

Data

What we observe

72,298
Pins in English LSOAs (43,939 liked | 28,359 disliked) from 79,182 participants | IoD 2025
49,190
Liked-place free-text reasons (QX) + 30,710 dislike reasons (QY)
~1.08M
Overture POIs across England; features computed in 800 m buffers around pins
  • IMD is measured at the pin LSOA - deprivation of the evaluated place, not of the participant. Higher IMD = more deprived.
  • Deprivation strata: High = IMD Q1-Q2, Low = Q4-Q5 (Q3 held out of binary contrasts).
  • Analysis combines deprivation scores, POI environments, and semantic themes from text.
Roadmap

Organised by argument, not by method

Section 1

Deprivation changes environments

Context differs.

Section 2

People prefer certain environments

Values are clear.

Section 3

Core valuations are shared

The centrepiece.

Section 1 | RQ1

Deprivation changes neighbourhood environments

Affluent and deprived neighbourhoods differ substantially. This is the context.

Section 1

Liked places are less deprived than disliked ones

Within person, the liked pin tends to sit in a less-deprived LSOA than the disliked pin - a systematic environmental gap, not a random scatter.

Deprivation reshapes the pool of places people put forward for evaluation - we observe chosen pins, not full daily exposure.

Liked vs disliked IMD score (higher = more deprived).

Section 1

Local environments also differ by deprivation

Around liked pins, POI accessibility and composition shift across IMD quintiles - green access, destinations, and urban intensity are not evenly distributed.

  • POI summary of what surrounds places
  • IMD gradients in neighbourhood scores

POI mix around pins.

Liked-pin environments by IMD quintile.

Section 1 | takeaway

Affluent and deprived neighbourhoods differ substantially in the environments on offer.

That is necessary context - not yet evidence about preferences.

Section 2 | RQ2

People consistently prefer certain environments

What do people value? POIs, themes, words, and examples - together.

Section 2

A clear evaluative grammar

Positive

  • Green / nature
  • Walking
  • Community
  • Peaceful, calm settings

Negative

  • Road / street
  • Station / transport intensity
  • Housing / estate
  • Derelict or disordered sites

Same story in distinctive words, embedding themes, and POI associations with Like.

Section 2

Words and themes tell the same story

Distinctive vocabulary: restorative vs infrastructural.

Theme like-share (Wilson 95% CIs).

Free-text uses dedicated survey fields: liked-place reasons (QX) and dislike reasons (QY). The POI evidence on the next slide is text-independent.

Section 2

Environments track those valuations

Green accessibility associates with higher odds of Like; transport-heavy settings track road complaints and negative place talk.

This is text-independent evidence: the Like outcome comes from pin behaviour, not from free-text. It answers what people value - not yet whether that depends on deprivation.

Like vs park proximity / green accessibility (+ IMD control).

Section 2 | takeaway

Across words, themes and neighbourhood features, people value green, walkable, communal places - and reject road- and estate-dominated ones.

Section 3 | RQ3 | novelty

Core valuations are shared across deprivation

Quantitative → statistical → qualitative. High deprivation = IMD Q1-Q2 | Low = Q4-Q5, at the pin LSOA - deprivation of the evaluated place, not of the person. (Home IMD is available for ~85% of participants as a person-level check.)

Section 3 | sequence

One centrepiece, four beats

01

Word scatter Do the same words mark Like vs Dislike in high and low deprivation?

02

Theme × IMD interactions Does deprivation change the relative preference for Nature vs Road?

03

Within-theme odds Among Nature pins only - and Road pins only - does IMD still predict Like?

04

Nature examples Do people describe parks in the same language across contexts?

Section 3 | words

The same words mark Like and Dislike

ρ ≈ 0.92
Like-Dislike word log-odds, high vs low deprivation (1,256 shared words)
90%
Words keep the same sign across strata
Restorative language stays positive; infrastructural language stays negative - in both deprived and affluent places.

Shared-vocabulary log-odds: high vs low deprivation.

Section 3 | interactions

Judge the interactions by their CIs, not p-values

Like ~ Theme × IMD, interaction ORs with 95% CIs - binary: Nature 1.47 [1.03-2.10], Road 1.84 [1.24-2.72]; continuous IMD z: Nature 1.18 [0.99-1.41], Road 1.29 [1.03-1.61].

  • With the larger sample, some Theme × IMD interactions are detectable - still modest ORs, not a preference reversal
  • Formal TOST at a pre-declared SESOI (OR band 0.67-1.5): continuous Nature × IMD remains equivalent (pTOST ≈ 0.004); Road continuous passes the looser OR-2 band
  • Joint Theme × IMD LR test is significant; 3/8 individual binary interactions p<0.05
  • Sharpest substantive evidence is still within-theme like shares (next slide): ~1 pp gaps

Theme × IMD interaction ORs; shaded band = SESOI [1/1.5, 1.5] (TOST).

Section 3 | within theme

Parks are liked; roads are disliked - in both strata

94% | 95%
Nature pins liked (high vs low deprivation; 94.1% / 95.0%)
3.3% | 4.0%
Road pins liked (high vs low deprivation)

The stratum gaps remain substantively small and precisely estimated: +0.9 pp for Nature (94.1% [92.3-95.5] vs 95.0% [93.9-95.9]) and +0.7 pp for Road (3.3% [2.4-4.5] vs 4.0% [3.3-5.0]), Wilson 95% CIs. Nature stays overwhelmingly liked and Road overwhelmingly disliked in both strata.

Within-theme like share by deprivation stratum.

Section 3 | examples

Nature is described in a shared lexicon

Liked Nature comments from high- and low-deprivation pins share restorative cues - peaceful, calm, quiet, green, bird, open (top-20 token Jaccard ≈ 0.82).

High-IMD and low-IMD parks live in essentially the same semantic space (Nature centroid cosine ≈ 0.995; Road ≈ 0.995).

Representative Nature reasons across deprivation.

Section 3 | takeaway

Core valuations (Nature liked; Road disliked) hold across place deprivation. Detectable Theme × IMD shifts are small in absolute like-share terms; unequal neighbourhoods still mainly change which environments people evaluate.

Scope of the claims

What this evidence is - and is not

Evaluation, not exposure

Pins are chosen evaluations, not daily mobility. We say “environments people evaluate.” Home postcode (PS2) is now linked for ~85% of participants as a person-level IMD check - still not full mobility.

Place and person deprivation

Primary RQ3 uses pin LSOA IMD (place). Home IMD analyses are a parallel person-level track; both keep Nature overwhelmingly liked.

Free-text fields

Liked and dislike reasons now use dedicated QX / QY fields. POI-Like associations remain text-independent corroboration.

Shared cores, small shifts

Continuous Nature × IMD remains TOST-equivalent at SESOI 0.67-1.5 (p ≈ 0.004). Some binary Theme × IMD terms are significant with larger N; within-theme like-share gaps stay ~1 pp.

Discussion

Not “people like green”

People share similar preferences, but unequal neighbourhoods offer unequal access to the environments people already value.

Opportunity, not taste

IMD gaps in liked vs disliked pins read as differences in the environments available to evaluate - not different preference functions.

Policy implication

Expanding access to the environments people already value may matter more than assuming different tastes by class.

Caveat

Consistency is strongest for Nature vs Road; some mixed themes show milder context effects.

Closing

Neighbourhood deprivation changes the environments people evaluate; core place valuations remain shared, with only small absolute Theme × IMD shifts.

Thank you
